path.title: What Is the Gospel
path.why: A newcomer needs the central announcement before a catalogue of controversies. This study also helps experienced readers distinguish the saving message from a promise of prosperity, a political program, or a technique for becoming a better person.
path.build: Create an opening path with four linked scenes: promise, cross, resurrection, and response. Each scene displays its passage in context; a final panel connects grace to discipleship without suggesting that deeds purchase salvation.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Christian traditions differ about how baptism, justification, and perseverance fit into receiving salvation. Do not hide those differences, but do not make a complete theory of salvation a prerequisite for understanding this announcement. Scripture does not prescribe one mandatory wording of a conversion prayer.

path.title: One God Father Son and Holy Spirit
path.why: It explains why Christians worship Jesus, pray to the Father through the Son, and speak of the Spirit as divine without confessing three gods. It also teaches readers how a responsible doctrine can arise through synthesis.
path.build: Use a passage-first matrix: unity, personal distinction, and divine identity. Open each cell to its full passage. Avoid water, egg, or three-person analogies as explanatory proofs because they readily imply changing modes or three separate gods.
path.guardrail: The synthesis has very strong canonical support, but classify the synthesis as inference. Do not rely on the disputed expanded wording of 1 John 5:7. Eastern and Western churches differ on the Spirit’s procession; that later disagreement requires separate historical treatment.

path.title: The Word Became Flesh
path.why: If Jesus only appeared human, his solidarity with people and his death would be emptied of meaning. This page helps readers hold together the Gospel narratives and the doctrinal claims about his identity.
path.build: Use two columns of textual evidence, divine identity and genuine humanity, joined to one central identity. A short historical layer can reveal later doctrinal vocabulary and the errors it was intended to exclude.
path.guardrail: Christians debate how divine knowledge relates to human growth and sayings such as Mark 13:32. The passages establish genuine humanity more securely than they explain its psychological mechanism. Oriental Orthodox traditions also confess full deity and humanity while historically disputing Chalcedonian terminology; do not caricature them as denying either.

path.title: The Cross in the Gospel Narratives
path.why: The cross is central to the gospel but can become an abstract symbol detached from the narratives. Reading the accounts closely allows doctrine to grow from what the texts actually narrate.
path.build: Use four Gospel columns aligned by narrated event, with differences preserved. Let users expand each account’s scriptural references and distinguish reported sequence from a proposed combined chronology.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Do not attribute collective guilt to Jewish people; the texts include varied Jewish actors and Roman authority, and Christian doctrine applies sin universally. The exact calendar date is debated. Do not build an interpretation on Luke 23:34 without noting that the prayer’s first sentence has a textual variant.

path.title: How the New Testament Explains Atonement
path.why: One image alone can flatten the Bible’s account. This study helps readers recognize how different passages address guilt, alienation, bondage, death, and transformed life without pretending that all Christian theories are identical.
path.build: Create a multi-entry diagram with the human predicament on one side and the relevant biblical image on the other. Every connection opens a paragraph and displays where the image stops explaining.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: The strongest conclusion is Christ’s decisive saving self-giving, with several complementary biblical descriptions. Debate remains over mechanism, scope, and how images fit together. Do not depict the Father as unwilling to forgive until a loving Son changes his mind: 2 Corinthians 5:19 locates reconciliation in God’s own action in Christ.

path.title: The Resurrection at the Center of Christian Hope
path.why: The resurrection is not an optional illustration of hope. Paul explicitly makes the truth of Christian proclamation and future resurrection depend on it, giving readers a clear sense of its doctrinal importance.
path.build: Link the narrated appearances to an argument map of 1 Corinthians 15: proclamation, counterfactual, firstfruits, and final victory. Keep disputed ordering of appearances visibly separate from the theological claims.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: The Gospels do not supply a single effortless combined sequence. Some appearances listed by Paul are not narrated elsewhere. Preserve those limits rather than inventing missing scenes. Bodily resurrection does not mean that every property of present mortal life remains unchanged.

path.title: Justification and Peace with God
path.why: This is a central doctrine for understanding salvation and a major place where Christians talk past one another. Close comparison lets readers see both shared affirmations and the remaining interpretive disagreements.
path.build: Create a comparison matrix of biblical text, question addressed, and each tradition’s interpretation. Display common ground first, then clarify which terms have different definitions.
path.guardrail: Editorial judgment: any adequate account must preserve unearned grace and the necessity of living faith. The precise relation of verdict and renewal remains debated. Avoid the caricature that Catholics teach salvation earned without grace or Protestants teach that transformed life is irrelevant.

path.title: Perseverance and the Warning Passages
path.why: This debate affects preaching, assurance, and care for people who fail. The study should keep promises and warnings together, allowing neither a careless presumption nor an interpretation that removes every ground for hope.
path.build: Build a side-by-side argument map in which every view must explain the same five passage units. Distinguish a view’s direct textual observations from its harmonizing inference.
path.guardrail: Editorial judgment: perseverance is necessary and God’s keeping is powerful; the texts should not be used to trivialize either. The logical reconciliation remains disputed. Hebrews' warning against repudiating Christ should not be equated with every lapse or unwanted thought.

path.title: Baptism and Belonging to Christ
path.why: The topic should begin with the range of biblical statements rather than a denominational definition alone. Readers can then see why baptism matters and why Christians disagree about language such as sign, means of grace, and regeneration.
path.build: Use a passage matrix with command, meaning, response, and community columns. Add tradition overlays while keeping the same passages visible to every reader.
path.guardrail: Editorial judgment: baptism is commanded and Christ-centered, with rich saving associations. The exact relation between sign, faith, and grace requires synthesis and remains disputed. Do not equate sacramental theology with magic or symbolic theology with the claim that baptism is unimportant.

path.title: The Lord's Supper Remembrance and Participation
path.why: This central Christian practice is both unifying and disputed. Its biblical setting exposes an often-neglected connection between eucharistic theology and how the church treats poor or excluded members.
path.build: Build a shared Scripture panel with tabs for remembrance, participation, covenant, and community. Below it compare each tradition’s account of presence, faith, and sacrifice using neutral definitions.
path.guardrail: Editorial judgment: the text requires more than a private mental reminder, including communal accountability; it does not supply the later metaphysical vocabulary by itself. Avoid saying that Catholic teaching re-crucifies Christ, or that every Protestant treats the meal as empty symbolism. John 6’s precise eucharistic relation is also debated.

path.title: Scripture Authority and Responsible Reading
path.why: A Bible-first project needs more than many citations. Readers must learn why context matters, how to distinguish a narrator’s report from approval, and why a verse cannot be made to answer every later question.
path.build: Create an interpretation workflow: read the paragraph, identify genre and speaker, locate the book’s argument, compare relevant passages, then distinguish observation from application. Show a worked example from Mark 7.
path.guardrail: The cited verses do not list every book of the canon or settle every doctrine of inerrancy. Scripture’s authority does not make a reader’s interpretation inerrant. Do not treat an isolated phrase from Job’s friends or a villain’s speech as an endorsed divine proposition.

path.title: A Library with a Story: How the Bible Fits Together
path.why: Readers often confuse the order printed in a Bible with the order of events. A book map gives newcomers a place to stand and prevents advanced cross-references from becoming disconnected verse collections.
path.build: Build a book shelf that switches between printed order, literary group, and narrated period. Each book opens a short contextual summary and three passage links; mark uncertain dates with ranges rather than a fixed point.
path.guardrail: "Old" does not mean worthless: Romans 15:4 explicitly gives earlier Scripture an ongoing purpose. Christian unity of Scripture should not erase Jewish readings or treat every Israelite institution as a coded prediction. Distinguish a book’s setting from its composition date.

path.title: The Torah: Rescue Before Rules
path.why: Leviticus becomes less alien when its holy dwelling stands inside the rescue story. Deuteronomy’s sermons make sense when heard by a generation about to live differently from its parents.
path.build: Create five connected panels, each with opening situation, turning point, ending location, and unanswered question. Selecting a command reveals its narrative setting and related New Testament discussion without replacing the Torah passage.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: This outline should not imply that grace begins only in the New Testament or that Christians apply every Mosaic command unchanged. Christian traditions distinguish covenant continuity and discontinuity differently; explore those debates separately through Matthew 5:17-20, Acts 15:1-29, and Galatians 3:15-29.

path.title: Exodus Routes: Plot the Evidence Before the Line
path.why: Emmaus already has an Exodus map. Its largest research opportunity is greater reliability: a confidently drawn line can conceal uncertain place identifications and make a popular hypothesis appear archaeologically established.
path.build: For each proposed line show source, dated publication, candidate-site evidence, chronological assumptions, and unresolved contradictions. Default to textual stages and uncertainty regions. Keep travel distance, terrain, and water calculations conditional on a selected, documented route.
path.guardrail: Editorial judgment: no consulted evidence establishes Nuweiba/Jabal al-Lawz as the leading alternative or fixes Sinai. Present it as one disputed proposal only if responsibly sourced; avoid decorative parity with better-studied candidates. Neither a traditional pilgrimage location nor a dramatic landscape establishes biblical identity.

path.title: Four Gospels, Four Narrated Routes into the Same Good News
path.why: A reader who knows only a blended life of Jesus can miss why a saying appears at a particular point. This module makes comparison serve close reading instead of erasing each evangelist’s argument.
path.build: Extend Emmaus’s book library with four horizontal reading tracks. Selecting a shared scene highlights each parallel while preserving surrounding paragraphs. A separate comparison drawer distinguishes agreement, omission, different wording, and genuine chronological tension.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Literary emphases are not exclusive ownership: all four Gospels include suffering, fulfillment, discipleship, and resurrection. The traditional author names should not be confused with explicit self-identification in each narrative. A harmony is a proposed synthesis, not a fifth canonical Gospel.

path.title: The Cross in Four Voices
path.why: Familiar devotional summaries often merge the seven sayings into a single sequence that no Gospel gives. A comparison teaches the theological richness of each account while keeping the textual evidence visible.
path.build: Create a four-column scene matrix with filters for speech, witnesses, mockery, Scripture, signs, and burial transition. Display the traditional seven-sayings collection as a devotional grouping with its proposed ordering clearly labeled.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Luke 23:34’s forgiveness saying has significant manuscript variation and belongs with a textual note, not silent certainty. No passage assigns collective guilt to every Jewish person. The narratives identify particular actors and also place the execution within Roman authority.

path.title: Resurrection Witnesses: What Each Account Actually Reports
path.why: The resurrection is foundational, but a neat harmonized chart can hide genuine differences in narrative detail. Transparent comparison strengthens literacy and prevents claims that depend on invented travel or unreported conversations.
path.build: Extend Emmaus’s Gospel material with columns for source, participants, place, time, actions, and certainty. Offer separate tracks for tomb discovery, appearances, and later visions. Connect each record to the source paragraph and show competing correlations without merging records automatically.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: The number and placement of angelic figures, women’s sequences, and Jerusalem/Galilee instructions require careful comparison. Mark 16:9-20 belongs in a visibly marked textual appendix. Editorial judgment: affirm what the sources state while leaving their complete combined chronology unresolved.

path.title: Paul's Journeys with Letters Attached and Dates Qualified
path.why: Readers can understand why a letter addresses particular people and crises when it sits beside ministry events. They also need to know which familiar missionary-journey labels are organizing conventions rather than phrases Paul uses for his life.
path.build: Add letter envelopes to existing route segments, clickable to show internal dating clues. Display date ranges, uncertain correlations, named companions, and planned routes. A switch hides all nonbiblical dates so readers can inspect the narrative sequence alone.
path.guardrail: Galatians 2’s visit is identified by interpreters with Acts 11 or Acts 15; that decision affects early chronology. Do not turn "first, second, third journey" into a complete account of every trip. Post-Acts ministry and later martyrdom belong in a separately sourced continuation.

path.title: Sennacherib and Hezekiah: Two Accounts of 701 BCE
path.why: This is an unusually rich case for learning how historical corroboration works. Agreement on rulers and conflict is substantial, while silence about an event and differences in numbers must be treated honestly.
path.build: Offer an event-alignment table with columns for Kings, Isaiah, and the prism. Highlight shared names and payments while placing silence, contradiction, and theological explanation in separate rows.
path.guardrail: One-campaign and multi-stage reconstructions attempt to explain narrative seams and tribute differences; the consulted evidence does not settle every chronological question. A plague explanation remains a hypothesis. Do not claim that the prism describes the angel of 2 Kings 19:35, or that royal silence proves every detail of the account.

path.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls: Continuity and Variation Together
path.why: The reader learns why textual criticism exists without equating variants with total textual uncertainty. A visible manuscript comparison can replace slogans about either flawless uniformity or wholesale corruption.
path.build: Provide a manuscript timeline and a controlled comparison of selected passages, classifying each difference as spelling, wording, expansion, or arrangement. A separate bookshelf panel distinguishes biblical works from other Qumran literature.
path.guardrail: Do not say every scroll came from the same community or that all Dead Sea finds date to the same centuries; other Judean Desert collections differ. The Essene association is influential but its extent remains debated. Digitized images do not remove the need for trained decipherment or establish the date of a book’s original composition.

path.title: The Census of Quirinius: An Honest Chronology Workshop
path.why: An advanced reference should show difficult historical questions plainly. The reader can distinguish Luke’s theological purpose and narrative claims from proposals made to reconcile them with external records.
path.build: Display two timelines with the independently attested anchors and a third layer for proposed reconciliations. A grammar panel should show why first and before translations are debated rather than treating one English rendering as decisive.
path.guardrail: An earlier census or earlier administrative role could reconcile the accounts but needs evidence not presently established. Reading the Greek as before Quirinius is a proposed grammatical solution, not the natural majority translation. A chronological conflation by Luke is the simplest historical explanation on the currently presented evidence; the exact mechanism remains uncertain and is distinct from a judgment on the whole Gospel.

path.title: Where Does Mark End? Manuscripts and Resurrection Witness
path.why: The passage is conspicuous in modern translation footnotes and sometimes used to unsettle readers. A careful comparison makes the actual uncertainty intelligible while keeping the resurrection announcement already present in Mark visible.
path.build: Create a manuscript-family overview with the short, long, and abrupt endings visible. Let readers see how Mark 14:28 and 16:7 point toward Galilee before they compare later ending traditions.
path.guardrail: Traditions differ in liturgical and canonical treatment, and some defenders emphasize widespread reception and early attestation. These matter historically but do not outweigh the combined case for secondary composition here. Do not build a distinctive snake-handling practice on this text; narrative signs are not an instruction to manufacture danger. Lost-ending versus intentional-ending theories remain uncertain.

path.title: Love of Neighbor Across Ethnic Boundaries
path.why: This study equips the site to address a central biblical theme without reducing it to modern slogans. It also demonstrates how story, command, and church decision illuminate one another.
path.build: Make a boundary-crossing map with characters, risk, cost, and outcome. Link the parable, Acts 10, and Acts 15 so users can compare individual mercy with institutional discernment.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: The church’s decisions in Acts 15 do not provide a simplistic template for every later dispute. Do not weaponize the passages to erase legitimate doctrinal differences or the continuing significance of Jewish Scripture.

path.title: The Kingdom Already Here and Still Coming
path.why: This is one of the most important organizing themes for Jesus' teaching and the whole Bible. It helps readers place parables, miracles, ethics, and hope on one timeline.
path.build: Use a kingdom timeline with present signs, hidden growth, ethical practices, and future judgment. Let users compare a parable’s temporal emphasis before reading an eschatological system.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Christian traditions disagree about the kingdom’s relation to the church, Israel, and millennium. All positions must address Jesus' present proclamation and future consummation.

path.title: Revelation's Throne Lamb and New Creation
path.why: Readers often approach Revelation as a codebook. A visual sequence can restore its worshipful, pastoral, and justice-centered purpose.
path.build: Build a scroll-to-city visual with worship, judgment, martyr witness, and healing layers. Add an Old Testament image index that shows repeated motifs without flattening every reuse into identical meaning.
path.deps: local Scripture and the site reading view
path.guardrail: Historicist, preterist, futurist, and idealist readings identify different relationships between visions and history. The book’s explicit calls to endurance and worship are clearer than a date chart for every headline event.

questions.q: When does a promise become a covenant?
questions.body: Compare divine promise, oath, sign, and covenant in Genesis 12, 15, 17, Exodus 19-24, and Hebrews 8.

questions.q: How should Christians read genealogies?
questions.body: Track literary, theological, and chronological functions in Genesis, Chronicles, Matthew, and Luke.

questions.q: Why does God ask Abraham to offer Isaac?
questions.body: Read Genesis 22 with promise, testing, substitution, and later biblical echoes kept distinct.

questions.q: What does "know" mean in the Bible?
questions.body: Study relational knowledge in Genesis 4, Amos 3, John 10, and 1 John 2 without reducing it to information.

questions.q: Is the conquest language literal, hyperbolic, or layered?
questions.body: Compare Joshua, Judges, Deuteronomy, and archaeological evidence while labeling every inference.

questions.q: What is the biblical meaning of rest?
questions.body: Follow Sabbath, land rest, Jesus, Hebrews 3-4, and the new creation.

questions.q: Why do prophets use marriage language?
questions.body: Trace covenant fidelity, accusation, judgment, and restoration in Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Revelation.

questions.q: What does "day of the LORD" include?
questions.body: Map near historical judgments and final hope across Joel, Amos, Zephaniah, and 2 Peter.

questions.q: Does wisdom promise a trouble-free life?
questions.body: Read Proverbs with Job and Ecclesiastes, then classify proverb, lament, and observation.

questions.q: Why are there two creation accounts?
questions.body: Compare Genesis 1 and 2 by genre, sequence, emphasis, and canonical purpose without inventing conflict.

questions.q: What is the image of God?
questions.body: Join Genesis 1, Psalm 8, James 3, and Colossians 3 to ask about dignity, vocation, and renewal.

questions.q: How does Scripture portray disability and healing?
questions.body: Read John 9, Mark 2, Leviticus 21, and 2 Samuel 9 with careful attention to stigma and agency.

questions.q: What is a biblical lament?
questions.body: Build a reusable grammar from complaint, memory, petition, trust, and praise.

questions.q: What does "fear of the LORD" mean?
questions.body: Compare reverence, terror, wisdom, and covenant loyalty across Proverbs, Exodus, and the Gospels.

questions.q: Why are angels unnamed in most scenes?
questions.body: Study messenger, worship, protection, and judgment without turning every angel into a personal guide.

questions.q: How should readers handle divine violence?
questions.body: Put conquest, judgment, patience, prophetic critique, cross, and final judgment into one evidence-graded workspace.

questions.q: What is the role of the stranger?
questions.body: Track resident foreigners, Rahab, Ruth, the Samaritan, Cornelius, and the nations in Revelation.

questions.q: How does the Bible discuss debt?
questions.body: Compare debt release, slavery, generosity, and Jesus economic parables; do not leap to a modern policy.

questions.q: What is biblical inheritance?
questions.body: Trace land, sonship, resurrection, and kingdom inheritance from Numbers to Romans and 1 Peter.

questions.q: Why does Jesus use meals so often?
questions.body: Map table fellowship, purity, honor, betrayal, Eucharist, and the marriage supper.

questions.q: What is the "kingdom of heaven"?
questions.body: Compare Matthew wording with Mark and Luke and distinguish kingdom, church, and final renewal.

questions.q: How does Jesus read the Psalms?
questions.body: Index Psalm quotations and allusions in the Gospels, Acts, and Hebrews.

questions.q: What is a parable allowed to do?
questions.body: Study ambiguity, reversal, judgment, and audience response rather than treating each detail as a code.

questions.q: How does the Spirit guide Acts?
questions.body: Map speeches, visions, prohibitions, prophecy, and communal decisions while preserving narrative tension.

questions.q: What is the relationship between faith and sight?
questions.body: Compare seeing signs, believing testimony, walking by faith, and final vision.

questions.q: How do Christians disagree about election?
questions.body: Place Calvinist, Arminian, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, and Wesleyan statements beside Romans 9, John 6, and 1 Timothy 2.

questions.q: What does "once for all" mean?
questions.body: Trace Hebrews, Romans, and 1 Peter on Christ sacrifice and the continuing life of obedience.

questions.q: How should the church handle money?
questions.body: Compare Acts 2-5, 1 Corinthians 16, 2 Corinthians 8-9, and 1 Timothy 6.

questions.q: What is spiritual warfare in the New Testament?
questions.body: Read temptation, exorcism, armor, suffering, and Revelation as distinct contexts.

questions.q: How does Scripture teach children?
questions.body: Study Deuteronomy 6, Psalm 78, Mark 10, Ephesians 6, and Timothy without assuming one family model.

questions.q: What is the biblical use of silence?
questions.body: Contrast silence as listening, grief, witness, withdrawal, and judgment.

questions.q: How do biblical writers quote one another?
questions.body: Build a quotation graph that records wording, context, and fulfillment claim.

questions.q: What does "all Israel" mean in Romans 11?
questions.body: Present major readings with the paragraph, Old Testament echoes, and denominational statements visible.

questions.q: How should Revelation be dated?
questions.body: Compare internal clues, early witnesses, and historical proposals; label certainty and disagreement.

questions.q: What is the meaning of the Lord's Day?
questions.body: Study Sabbath, resurrection, assembly, and later Christian practice without assuming a single timeline.

questions.q: How can a study avoid proof texting?
questions.body: Turn the responsible workflow into an interactive checklist with a required context and caveat field.

questions.q: What does biblical justice require?
questions.body: Map courts, impartiality, gleaning, prophets, Jesus, James, and final judgment.

questions.q: What is the Bible's theology of work?
questions.body: Connect creation vocation, Sabbath, craft, idleness, labor dignity, and new creation.

questions.q: How does God respond to doubt?
questions.body: Compare Gideon, Psalms, Habakkuk, Thomas, and Jude with different kinds of uncertainty.

questions.q: What makes a witness credible?
questions.body: Study two witnesses, apostolic testimony, women at the tomb, public signs, and the Spirit’s witness.

questions.q: Why does the New Testament never cite Isaiah 9:6?
questions.body: Compare the passages the apostles quote with the ones Christians quote most; ask what the difference reveals about apostolic reading.

questions.q: Was the temple curtain the inner one or the outer one?
questions.body: Weigh Hebrews 10:20, Josephus’s description, and Matthew’s cosmic signs; decide what each option would mean.

questions.q: What did Jesus's hearers think a 'kingdom of priests' meant?
questions.body: Trace Exodus 19:6 through Isaiah 61:6, 1 Peter 2:9, and Revelation 1:6; test whether the phrase describes status, function, or both.

questions.q: How reliable are the psalm headings?
questions.body: Compare Hebrew, Septuagint, and Qumran headings; ask what a heading claims and what it cannot establish.

questions.q: Why is Melchizedek given no genealogy?
questions.body: Read Genesis 14, Psalm 110, and Hebrews 7 with attention to what Hebrews argues from silence, and where that method has limits.

questions.q: Did Israel's camp really form a cross?
questions.body: Compute the tribal totals, draw the camp to scale, and ask what a modern shape observation can and cannot mean.

questions.q: What is the relationship between Ezekiel's temple and Revelation's city?
questions.body: List every shared image and every difference, especially the absence of a temple in Revelation 21:22.

questions.q: Which 'Mary' is which?
questions.body: Sort the six or seven Marys of the New Testament by Gospel and scene; identify where identifications are certain, probable, or guessed.

questions.q: How did money changers actually operate in the temple?
questions.body: Combine Exodus 30, the Tyrian shekel requirement, Mishnah Shekalim, and the Gospel accounts; separate evidence from assumption about Jesus’s motive.

questions.q: What should a site do with a beloved claim it cannot verify?
questions.body: Use the kezazah, the four-inch curtain, and the 153 species as test cases for an editorial policy on popular illustrations.

confirmed: Archaeological dates and discoverers: Tel Dan stele (1993-94, Biran; ninth century BCE); Mesha stele (Dhiban, ninth century); Lachish reliefs (Room XXXVI, Nineveh, campaign of 701 BCE); Taylor Prism (691 BCE, acquired 1855); Cyrus Cylinder (Rassam, 1879; after 539 BCE); Pilate stone (Frova, Caesarea, 1961); Merneptah stele (Petrie, 1896; year 5, about 1208 BCE); Hezekiah bulla (Ophel, 2009 excavation, announced 2015); Ketef Hinnom amulets (Barkay, 1979); Pool of Siloam steps (Reich and Shukron, 2004); Delphi Gallio inscription (52 CE).

Historical dates: Samaria’s fall (722 BCE); Jerusalem’s capture (597) and destruction (587/586); Cyrus’s capture of Babylon (539); temple rededication under the Maccabees (164 BCE); the Quirinius census (6 CE) against Herod’s death (4 BCE standard); Council of Chalcedon (451).
Canon counts: Protestant 39 + 27; Catholic 46 + 27; Jewish 24-book grouping of the same Hebrew books.
Textual judgments in A023-A028 (Deuteronomy 32:8, Mark 16, John 7:53-8:11, 1 John 5:7, Goliath’s height, Psalm 22:16) match the NET notes and standard critical editions.

Radiocarbon dating of Jericho’s Middle Bronze destruction to the late seventeenth or sixteenth century BCE (Bruins and van der Plicht), with the about-1400 BCE proposal correctly labeled a minority reassessment.
corrected: Fifteen entries (L003, L005, L006, L009, L010, L013, L018, L033, N001, N007, N009, N028, N029, A016, A020) carried the value 'Bible Literacy' in their Difficulty field, which is a category name, not a level. Each has been reset to Foundational; review individually if a different level is intended.
In 72 entries the Source Notes had been run into the Caveats and Limits paragraph during the original layout. They are now separated into their own labeled block.

Flagship 07 and the prophecy discussions referred generally to fulfillment; E017 now supplies the counting method and the caution about the popular '300 prophecies' figure, which has no single scholarly source.
flagged: Popular claims deliberately downgraded in the new entries: the kezazah ceremony (E033), the 'four-inch curtain horses could not tear' (E030), Jerome’s 153 fish species (E032), the 'gospel in the names of Genesis 5' (E010), the cruciform camp as prophecy (E001), Boaz and Joseph as formal 'types of Christ' (E021, E024), and the round rolling stone (E065).

Contested chronologies left visibly open: Exodus date and route (L016, A011), Ezra’s date (E014), Daniel’s seventy weeks (E019), Herod’s death year (E055), Pauline letter dates (E063), and the divergence of Matthew’s and Luke’s genealogies (E010).
Mishnaic measurements (soreg height, curtain dimensions, court sizes) are labeled as tradition compiled about 200 CE, not as first-century measurement (E004, E030).

Unprovenanced or disputed artifacts are graded lower than excavated ones: the 2011 'Miriam daughter of Yeshua' ossuary (E051), the Al-Yahudu tablets (E053), the Alexander son of Simon ossuary identification (E035), and the Talpiot tomb claims (E065).

audit: What the audit shows. Existing resources fall into two groups: visually strong but shallow (devotional graphics, most map sets) or scholarly but text-heavy (commentaries, translator notes, museum records). Very few combine original, accurate, tiered visuals with first-century context and honest handling of disputed questions. That combination is Emmaus’s opening. The licensing rule that follows from the audit is simple: generate original maps and diagrams from the biblical text and from tools whose output is unrestricted; use noncommercial assets only while the site is noncommercial; embed museum images by link; never trace copyrighted charts.
